topic.name: Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms: Determining Where Extrema are Attained

question.text: The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2-6x_1x_2,$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the maximum is attained?
question.explanation:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$ \[ \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}} \] The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

  • The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A{:}$ \[ \min \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{min}} \] The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}= 4{:}$

\begin{align*} A - 4 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A- 4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get

\[ \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} }{\| \mathbf{v} \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= 2x_1^2-x_2^2-x_3^2-2x_2x_3,$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1,$ is equal to $2.$ Which of the following is a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the maximum is attained?
question.explanation:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$ \[ \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}} \] The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

  • The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A{:}$ \[ \min \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{min}} \] The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=2{:}$

\begin{align*} A - 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: Find the maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-18x_1x_2+81x_2^2$ given that $x_1^2 + 9x_2^2=9.$
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81 \end{bmatrix} \]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

\[ \dfrac{x_1^2}{3^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{1^2}=1 \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the $x_2$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1=\dfrac{x_1}{3} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = {x_2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

\[ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y} = Q'(\mathbf{y}). \]

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

\begin{align*} B &= P^T \! AP \\[5pt] &= PAP \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 9& -27 \\ - 27 & 81 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, we maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} |B - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 9-\lambda & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] (9-\lambda)(81-\lambda) - 729 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 - 90 \lambda &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda (\lambda -90) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 0, \, 90 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\[ \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}} = 90. \]

question.text: The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=4x_1^2+4x_1x_2+x_2^2,$ when $9x_1^2+4x_2^2=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the maximum is attained?
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

\[ \dfrac{x_1^2}{2^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{3^2}=1 \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the $x_2$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1=\dfrac{x_1}{2} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \]

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

\[ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}). \]

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

\begin{align*} B &= P^T \! AP \\[5pt] &= PAP \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, we maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

\[ \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 25. \]

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=25{:}$

\begin{align*} B - 25 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9 \end{bmatrix} - 25 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = 5,$ we get

\[ \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\| \mathbf{v} \|} = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_{\textrm{max}} &= P \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text: The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2+8x_1x_2+8x_2^2,$ when $x_1^2+4x_2^2=4,$ is $12.$ Find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the maximum is attained.
question.explanation:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

\[ \dfrac{x_1^2}{2^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{1^2}=1 \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the $x_2$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1=\dfrac{x_1}{2} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = {x_2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

\[ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}). \]

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

\begin{align*} B &= P^T \! AP \\[5pt] &= PAP \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 8 \\ 8 &8 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, we maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $|| \mathbf{y} ||=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $12,$ we have

\[ \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 12. \]

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=12{:}$

\begin{align*} B - 12 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 8 \\ 8 &8 \end{bmatrix} - 12 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -16 & 8 \\ 8 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-12I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get

\[ \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\| \mathbf{v} \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_{\textrm{max}} &= P \mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
